fetched_contents.text: The Presence of Women in the Dental Profession: A Global Survey Abstract Objectives The aim of this research was to acquire knowledge about the female dental workforce, identifying factors to pursue specialty training and career choices and working in dental institutions/associations. Methods An original online questionnaire was developed, validated (n = 22), and sent to 189 member associations in 133 countries of the Women Dentists Worldwide section of the FDI World Dental Federation. Results In all, 3232 female dentists from 81 countries participated. Results were divided into 5 geographic areas by continent. Difference in proportion amongst questionnaire items was evaluated with χ2 test or Fisher exact test. Ordinal multinomial linear regression analysis was performed to evaluate the association of questionnaire items with total work experience in dentistry (in years), motivation to study dentistry, type of specialisation, working hours per week, perception of female dentists about working hours, sex-based inequalities, job security after maternity leaves, as well as involvement in political organisations within their country of residence and their role in dental associations. A majority of participating female dentists are self-employed (57.7%), and 60.0% have 10 to 30 years of experience. The most popular form of practice is the single private practice (29.7%), followed by the group private practice (28.8%). Further, 44.8% work 31 to 40 h/wk, 29.1% part-time up to 30 h/wk, and 26.0% more than 40 h/wk. Conclusions Women are still poorly represented in professional organisations, and few are officers in representative assemblies, members of the board, or president. Family life with children influences perceptions and has an impact on professional life, especially in academia and political/professional associations, so that taking on leadership positions poses additional challenges. Key words: Dentistry, Difference, Female dentist, Gender, Global oral health, Women dentists Introduction As in several health care professions, dentistry has been dominated by male representatives; recently, this trend has changed due to an increasing number of women being admitted to dental schools.1,2 The treatment of oral and other noncommunicable diseases places an enormous economic burden on health care systems worldwide.3, 4, 5, 6 In Europe, for example, 5 different health care systems can be distinguished.4 In most countries, the dental health system is on a private basis; however, even in the European union with 27 countries oral health care is organised independently and subsidiarily by nation-states.4 Currently, women make up between 48% and 75% of the dentist workforce7; proportions of male and female graduates are near the same in several world areas (ie, North America, Europe), whilst in other areas the gender gap has narrowed but is still present (ie, Oceania, Asia, Africa).7,8 However, the number of females in leading positions is significantly lower than male representatives; for example, in the US, women hold only as little as 18% of dental school dean positions and are 14% of division chiefs and department chairs.9 Female general dental practitioners are significantly less likely to have their own practice and/or become a partner in one as well as to be consultants in hospital dental settings.10 Female dentists are less likely to pursue postgraduate qualifications, and the average annual income of full-time self-employed women was 37% lower than the income of full-time self-employed men, which demonstrates the persistence of the gender-based wage gap.11 Usually, women take on additional responsibilities in the family, and male dentists take higher positions in academic institutions and dental organisations.12 Discrepancies of rights and policy statements in pregnancy, maternity leave, continued payment of wages, taxes, and pensions exist not only between employees and the self-employed, but also in international comparisons of nation-states.13 Worldwide differences in maternity leave and a lack of uniformity in parental leave policies are present, and negative effects of parenthood on well-being and work are more prevalent amongst female dentists than amongst male dentists.14,15 The FDI Section Women Dentists Worldwide (WDW)16 of the FDI World Dental Federation is responsible for coordinating the activities of national member associations, gathering information about women dentists and their practices, and promoting them. The Section is also committed to reaching out and facilitating contacts between women dentists worldwide to eliminate existing inequalities and to promote the full participation of women in all aspects of the dental profession.16 To try to bridge the gap on the presence of women in the dental profession, an international survey in collaboration with the FDI WDW Section on the presence of women in the profession was designed. The goals were to (1) gain knowledge about the female dental workforce and (2) establish information about specialty training, working in dental institutions, members and leaders of dental associations, general assemblies, and dental faculties. fetched_contents.text: Impact of Social Media on Aesthetic Dentistry: General Practitioners’ Perspectives Abstract The objective of this study was to investigate general dentists’ observations of various aesthetic dental procedures among social media users. A cross-sectional study was conducted at the Department of Prosthodontics, Altamash Institute of Dental Medicine, over a duration of six months. Data were collected using a well-structured questionnaire comprising 21 predefined responses. The questionnaire was uploaded and disseminated through Google Surveys by forwarding web page links through emails and WhatsApp. The data collected were analysed through Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS-Version 25). The majority (90.7%) of the dental practitioners surveyed believed that there is an increase in the demand for aesthetic dental procedures and social media is a major contributor to it. Moreover, most of the 377 (81.8%) participants agreed that social media is a beneficial platform enabling them to educate, advertise, and communicate with patients. Concerning popular aesthetic procedures, teeth whitening (54.7%), Hollywood smile (17.1%), dental veneers (11.9%), and Invisalign (10.4%) were the most commonly demanded aesthetic procedures. The patients showed desire for these procedures because they were trending on social media platforms. Almost half of the general dental practitioners used social media to post their content related to aesthetic dentistry and to promote their work. They preferred using before and after pictures (48.6%) for advertising their content related to aesthetic dentistry. Within the limitations of the study, it is concluded that the demand for aesthetic dentistry is rapidly growing, and social media is the main driving force behind this revolution as the general population has direct access to the profiles of celebrities and influencers, who all appear to have ‘the perfect smile’. This shift in people’s self-image has created a surge in patients seeking cosmetic treatments. Keywords: social media, aesthetic dentistry, dentists, WhatsApp 1. Introduction Dentistry is a science-based, highly structured healthcare profession that serves progressively more demanding patients [1]. The dental profession was once looked upon as a health sector that only operated to provide treatment of pain, jaws, gums or any other oral cavity diseases. The reason to seek dental care was solely for conventional treatments and patients consulted dentists only when there was an obvious need. Now, with the world changing, it cannot be denied that science and technology has advanced, and this has aided the healthcare system substantially; the medical field has come a long way and dentistry is no exception. Procedures and equipment have evolved extensively [2]. Today, dentistry is not only limited to procedures to treat the ill-fated tooth: elective aesthetic procedures are also being carried out [3]. Aesthetics and physical appearance are imperative attributes that cannot stay unnoticed and contribute to an individual’s personality. A beautiful smile with pearl white teeth framed by perfectly shaped lips makes one appear younger and socially more appealing. Moreover, features such as a defined jaw line, flawless skin, plumped lips, Hollywood smile, contoured nose, and other physically attractive aspects contribute to a person’s confidence level and boost one’s self-esteem [4]. The inclination towards aesthetic dentistry is rapidly growing most certainly because of increased social media usage in the present world, hence making it mandatory for dentists to offer procedures including veneer placements to mimic the Hollywood smile, orthodontic treatment to straighten teeth, and orthognathic surgery when there are extreme dentofacial anomalies that cannot be treated by orthodontic treatment, including corrective bone operations involving mobility of the jawbones. Facial proportions, lip balance, chin−nose balance, nasolabial angle and cheek implants are achieved by orthognathic surgery as well. Moreover, bleaching procedures to whiten teeth, reduction of irregular gum appearance in a smile, Botox to give a fuller look to lips, plasma-rich protein treatments, and many other procedures related to aesthetics are offered in order to satisfy patients: further, the pre-visualisation of the result makes the aesthetic operation more attractive [3,4,5,6,7]. It was observed over time that in some patients, the main aim of any procedure or even orthognathic surgery was to improve their physical attractiveness; extreme abnormalities or deformity made them feel aesthetically vulnerable in the age of social media and they sought social acceptance [5,6,7,8,9]. In this era, social media has the power to modify people’s way of thinking. It does not only showcase an image of beauty but has several passive effects too. Millions of people rely on social media platforms, such as Facebook, Snapchat, YouTube, Twitter, and Instagram to stay updated with the current news [10]. Hegarty et al. conducted a study in which they evaluated the top 60 videos related to orthognathic surgery and found that they had a combined total of 6,986,141 views. Evidence on young women’s actual and perceived demand for orthodontics versus medical aesthetics

The evidence base here is uneven: it is strong on drivers of demand and social media influence, weaker on direct comparative proportions of young women citing orthodontics versus medical aesthetics, and limited on explicit 20-30-year-old female samples. The strongest direct evidence comes from aesthetic dentistry and social media studies, which show that aesthetic procedures are rising rapidly and that social media is a major driver, with teeth whitening, Hollywood smile, veneers, and Invisalign among the most commonly demanded procedures [N2-F2]. In that study, 90.7% of surveyed dentists believed demand for aesthetic procedures is increasing, and social media is a major contributor, with before-and-after pictures used for advertising [N2-F2].

For orthodontics, the evidence points to growing adult orthodontic demand and strong aesthetic motivations. A 2025 source notes that Gen Z adults prioritize aesthetics, wellness, and personal branding, making orthodontics a “natural fit for their lifestyle” [N1-R3]. A separate 2025 source states that the number of adults seeing an orthodontist is at an all-time high, with one-in-three orthodontic patients over the age of 18 [N7-R4]. That indicates broad adult orthodontic uptake, but the evidence does not specify how many young women versus young women seeking medical aesthetics are included in that trend.

On priority drivers, the evidence is consistent across sources: self-esteem, smile appearance, social pressure, and career appearance are central. The aesthetic dentistry social media study frames the demand shift as linked to social media’s power to modify self-image, with patients seeking treatments because they are trending on platforms and because celebrities and influencers appear to have “the perfect smile” [N2-F2]. Another source notes that cosmetic dental procedures provide “emotional and social advantages” by improving the appearance of teeth and boosting self-esteem [N2-R5]. The same source also links demand to self-image and the desire to “live life to it’s fullest,” showing that the perceived value is not just functional but socially expressive [N2-R2]. A separate medical aesthetics source notes that 20-somethings are paying large sums for cosmetic procedures, with motivations including self-esteem, societal standards, and preference for minimally invasive options [N4-R4]. A further source highlights work-from-home trends among 20s and 30s age groups, with more time in front of cameras and mirrors driving demand for facial fillers [N4-R5]. Taken together, these sources support a driver set centered on appearance, social acceptance, and personal branding, rather than a single dominant motive.

Evidence gaps are substantial. First, the evidence is sparse on direct comparative proportions of young women citing orthodontics versus medical aesthetics as top concerns. The available evidence is mostly aggregated at the dentist or practitioner level, not at the individual consumer level, so it cannot reliably answer “proportion of young women citing orthodontics” versus “proportion citing medical aesthetics” [N2-F2; N1-R3]. Second, the evidence is regionally limited. The aesthetic dentistry survey was conducted in a single institutional setting in Pakistan and reported 377 dentists, while the broader market sources are global in scope but do not isolate 20-30-year-old women [N2-F2; N1-R2; N1-R4]. Third, there is no explicit longitudinal data across age groups in the provided evidence, so it is hard to assess whether orthodontic and medical aesthetic demand evolves differently over time or by cohort [N1-F1; N8-R2]. Fourth, the evidence is thin on region-specific or socioeconomic variables: the female dental workforce survey covers global participation and gender dynamics, but it does not isolate young women’s treatment preferences or access barriers by region or income level [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence supports a strong demand narrative, but it is not yet sufficient to quantify a precise proportion of young women prioritizing one modality over the other.

Market and behavioral evidence on how young women access and pay for orthodontic and aesthetic treatments

The evidence supports a market in which young women are increasingly active, but the payment models, frequency, and barriers are unevenly documented. On treatment frequency and payment models, the strongest evidence is that cosmetic procedures among 20-somethings are rising, with people under 30 in the US shelling out thousands of dollars for fillers, skin resurfacing treatments, and related procedures [N4-R1; N4-R3]. Another source notes that 20-somethings are paying up for cosmetic procedures to prevent aging, reinforcing that the market is not just one-time but ongoing [N4-R1; N4-R3]. This suggests a pattern of repeated or cumulative spending, though the evidence does not specify frequency by treatment type. For orthodontics, the evidence is more focused on adoption than on frequency. A 2026 market report states that the global orthodontic braces market grew at 13.87% CAGR during 2021–2024 and was valued at USD 21.42 billion in 2024 [N3-R2], while a separate 2026 report estimates the global orthodontic services market at USD 8.98 billion in 2026 and projects USD 20.48 billion by 2033 [N3-R4]. These figures suggest substantial market growth, but they do not directly measure how often young women use orthodontic services or how they finance them.

Willingness to pay is partially documented. A comparative study of young adults’ preferences and willingness to pay for accelerated orthodontic treatment found that about 70% of respondents were unwilling to pay more than 10% to 20% for all procedures assessed, and considerable variation was not observed in responses [N7-R2]. A separate willingness-to-pay study on adult orthodontics aimed to explore public and dental professional valuation of orthodontic services, but the excerpt provided does not give numerical willingness-to-pay figures [N7-R3]. Still, these sources together indicate that young adults are price-sensitive, with many reluctant to pay premiums even for accelerated or more advanced options [N7-R2]. The orthodontic market growth evidence also implies that non-traditional financing or payment models may be important, because the market is expanding alongside increased awareness, technological improvements, and social media influence [N3-R3]. However, the provided evidence does not explicitly name financing products, insurance coverage, or non-traditional payment structures, so that inference is limited.

The role of influencers, platforms, and non-traditional financing is supported by the aesthetic dentistry evidence. The social media study found that social media is a major contributor to demand and that dentists use before-and-after pictures for advertising content [N2-F2]. It also notes that patients are influenced by the profiles of celebrities and influencers who appear to have “the perfect smile,” which creates a surge in patients seeking cosmetic treatments [N2-F2]. The same source mentions that social media platforms such as Facebook, Snapchat, YouTube, Twitter, and Instagram are used by millions to stay updated with current news, and that the top 60 videos related to orthognathic surgery had a large combined audience [N2-F2]. This suggests that platforms are not only promotional but also shaping public perception and treatment expectations. The medical aesthetics source also notes that motivations include societal standards and preference for minimally invasive options, which implies that younger women may be influenced by platform-driven trends toward subtle, quick results [N4-R4].

Barriers are also evident, though not exhaustively quantified. Cost is clearly a barrier, because willingness-to-pay studies show reluctance to pay premiums and because cosmetic procedures can cost thousands of dollars [N4-R1; N4-R3; N7-R2]. Time is another barrier, as the orthodontic market growth is linked to convenience and discreet treatment options [N3-R3; N1-R5]. The social media study also notes that social media can create a shift in self-image that makes patients seek treatments, but it does not directly address stigma or access constraints [N2-F2]. The female dental workforce survey provides broader context on professional barriers, including maternity leave, wage gaps, and gender-based inequalities, which may indirectly affect young women’s access to care if these issues shape workforce availability or patient-provider interactions [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence suggests a market where young women are active and influenced by platforms, but cost, time, and social/structural barriers remain important constraints.

Clinical/technological and market potential for merging orthodontics with aesthetic medicine

The evidence supports the idea that orthodontics and aesthetic medicine are already converging in practice, and that technology and multidisciplinary models are enabling that convergence. On combined treatments and multidisciplinary clinics, the evidence shows that restorative dentistry and orthodontics can be combined to address complex full-mouth reconstruction cases [N5-R4]. A case study example also exists: an interdisciplinary orthodontic-aesthetic makeover treatment for a patient with maxillary lateral incisor agenesis and class II div. 2 malocclusion used space closure and other aesthetic interventions [N5-R5]. These examples suggest that integrated clinics or collaborative treatment models are not theoretical but are already being used, at least in selected cases.

Technological enablers are well represented. Digital twin technology is cited as integrating growth prediction models to enhance treatment planning for adolescent patients [N5-R1]. The 2026 orthodontics blog notes that the future of orthodontics is more efficient, comfortable, and personalized, driven by digital technology [N5-R3]. This indicates that digital workflows, simulation, and personalized planning are part of the convergence. The interdisciplinary orthodontic-restorative study further points to novel workflows that combine specialties, implying that digital coordination and shared treatment planning are becoming standard [N5-R4]. The evidence does not explicitly name AI or telehealth in the excerpts provided, but the presence of digital twin technology and workflow integration strongly suggests that AI-assisted diagnosis, predictive modeling, and remote communication are plausible future enablers [N5-R1; N5-R3]. In other words, the technological foundation is present, though the excerpts do not exhaustively detail all the digital tools.

The likelihood of future growth appears high, but the evidence also notes important limitations. Market growth is strong: orthodontic braces had a CAGR of 13.87% during 2021–2024, while orthodontic services are projected to reach USD 20.48 billion by 2033 [N3-R2; N3-R4]. Cosmetic dentistry is also growing rapidly, with market value crossing $31 billion in 2026 and projected to double by 2030 [N1-R2; N1-R4]. This suggests that the demand environment is favorable for convergence. However, the evidence on limitations is also clear. Methodological issues in clear aligner research include how outcomes are evaluated, with most studies comparing predicted and achieved tooth movement [N8-R3]. A scoping review also notes diversity in treatment types and methodological limitations, which can introduce heterogeneity and reduce generalizability [N8-R2]. The ethical and regulatory review emphasizes that aesthetic medicine has ethical dimensions and that consumer demand, societal influence, and technology are all relevant to the field [N6-R1]. It also highlights consent, confidentiality, and transparency as essential ethical care requirements [N6-R2]. Together, these limitations suggest that while the clinical and technological potential is real, the field remains constrained by methodological inconsistency, ethical complexity, and regulatory uncertainty.

Overall, the evidence supports a cautious but optimistic view of future growth: orthodontics and aesthetic medicine are already being merged in some clinics and workflows, digital tools are enabling more personalized planning, and market growth is strong. But the evidence also shows that current limitations include methodological weaknesses, ethical considerations, and the need for clearer regulatory boundaries [N5-R1; N5-R4; N6-R1; N6-R2; N8-R2].

The evidence points to several major gaps and limitations. First, there is a lack of longitudinal or comparative data across age groups. Second, the evidence is missing region-specific or socioeconomic data. The female dental workforce survey covers global female participation and gender dynamics, but it does not isolate young women’s treatment preferences, access, or socioeconomic barriers [N1-F1]. The medical aesthetics and orthodontic sources are global in scope but do not break out data by region, income level, or cultural context [N4-R1; N4-R3; N4-R4; N7-R4]. Third, ethical, legal, and reimbursement boundaries are not fully documented in the provided evidence. The ethical review discusses consumer demand, societal influences, and technology, but it does not provide a comprehensive reimbursement analysis [N6-R1]. The legal considerations source mentions consent, confidentiality, and transparency as ethical requirements, but it does not address legal liability, insurance coverage, or reimbursement policy differences across countries [N6-R2]. The Nuffield Council on Bioethics and other ethical sources highlight broader concerns about cosmetic procedures, but again, the evidence provided does not synthesize reimbursement or legal frameworks across jurisdictions [N6-R4; N6-R5].

Cost is clearly a barrier, because willingness-to-pay studies show reluctance to pay premiums and because cosmetic procedures can cost thousands of dollars [N4-R1; N4-R3; N7-R2]. Time is another barrier, as the orthodontic market growth is linked to convenience and discreet treatment options [N3-R3; N1-R5]. The social media study also notes that social media can create a shift in self-image that makes patients seek treatments, but it does not directly address stigma or access constraints [N2-F2]. The female dental workforce survey provides broader context on professional barriers, including maternity leave, wage gaps, and gender-based inequalities, which may indirectly affect young women’s access to care if these issues shape workforce availability or patient-provider interactions [N1-F1].

## 4) Clinical/technological and market potential for merging orthodontics with aesthetic medicine

The evidence supports the idea that orthodontics and aesthetic medicine are already converging in practice, and that technology and multidisciplinary models are enabling that convergence. On combined treatments and multidisciplinary clinics, the evidence shows that restorative dentistry and orthodontics can be combined to address complex full-mouth reconstruction cases [N5-R4]. A case study example also exists: an interdisciplinary orthodontic-aesthetic makeover treatment for a patient with maxillary lateral incisor agenesis and class II div. 2 malocclusion used space closure and other aesthetic interventions [N5-R5]. These examples suggest that integrated clinics or collaborative treatment models are not theoretical but are already being used, at least in selected cases.

Technological enablers are well represented. Digital twin technology is cited as integrating growth prediction models to enhance treatment planning for adolescent patients [N5-R1]. The 2026 orthodontics blog notes that the future of orthodontics is more efficient, comfortable, and personalized, driven by digital technology [N5-R3]. This indicates that digital workflows, simulation, and personalized planning are part of the convergence. The interdisciplinary orthodontic-restorative study further points to novel workflows that combine specialties, implying that digital coordination and shared treatment planning are becoming standard [N5-R4]. The evidence does not explicitly name AI or telehealth in the excerpts provided, but the presence of digital twin technology and workflow integration strongly suggests that AI-assisted diagnosis, predictive modeling, and remote communication are plausible future enablers [N5-R1; N5-R3]. In other words, the technological foundation is present, though the excerpts do not exhaustively detail all the digital tools.

The likelihood of future growth appears high, but the evidence also notes important limitations. Market growth is strong: orthodontic braces had a CAGR of 13.87% during 2021–2024, while orthodontic services are projected to reach USD 20.48 billion by 2033 [N3-R2; N3-R4]. Cosmetic dentistry is also growing rapidly, with market value crossing $31 billion in 2026 and projected to double by 2030 [N1-R2; N1-R4]. This suggests that the demand environment is favorable for convergence. However, the evidence on limitations is also clear. Methodological issues in clear aligner research include how outcomes are evaluated, with most studies comparing predicted and achieved tooth movement [N8-R3]. A scoping review also notes diversity in treatment types and methodological limitations, which can introduce heterogeneity and reduce generalizability [N8-R2]. The ethical and regulatory review emphasizes that aesthetic medicine has ethical dimensions and that consumer demand, societal influence, and technology are all relevant to the field [N6-R1]. It also highlights consent, confidentiality, and transparency as essential ethical care requirements [N6-R2]. Together, these limitations suggest that while the clinical and technological potential is real, the field remains constrained by methodological inconsistency, ethical complexity, and regulatory uncertainty.

## 5) Evidence gaps and limitations

The evidence points to several major gaps and limitations. First, there is a lack of longitudinal or comparative data across age groups. The provided evidence includes growth projections and market reports, but these are not longitudinal tracking studies comparing orthodontic and aesthetic demand by age over time [N1-R2; N1-R4; N3-R2; N3-R4]. The aesthetic dentistry survey is one-time and dentist-focused rather than consumer-centric, so it cannot establish age-group trends [N2-F2]. The orthodontic market reports similarly describe current or projected market size, not longitudinal cohort-level demand changes [N3-R2; N3-R4]. Second, the evidence is missing region-specific or socioeconomic data. The female dental workforce survey covers global female participation and gender dynamics, but it does not isolate young women’s treatment preferences, access, or socioeconomic barriers [N1-F1]. The medical aesthetics and orthodontic sources are global in scope but do not break out data by region, income level, or cultural context [N4-R1; N4-R3; N4-R4; N7-R4]. Third, ethical, legal, and reimbursement boundaries are not fully documented in the provided evidence. The ethical review discusses consumer demand, societal influences, and technology, but it does not provide a comprehensive reimbursement analysis [N6-R1]. The legal considerations source mentions consent, confidentiality, and transparency as ethical requirements, but it does not address legal liability, insurance coverage, or reimbursement policy differences across countries [N6-R2]. The Nuffield Council on Bioethics and other ethical sources highlight broader concerns about cosmetic procedures, but again, the evidence provided does not synthesize reimbursement or legal frameworks across jurisdictions [N6-R4; N6-R5].

The methodological limitations are also important. The scoping review notes that including a variety of TMD types and combinations can introduce heterogeneity and reduce comparability [N8-R2]. The clear aligner research source states that core methodological concerns are how outcomes are evaluated, particularly comparisons of predicted versus achieved tooth movement [N8-R3]. The aesthetic and orthodontic treatment desires study notes psychosocial impacts and relationships with treatment desire, but its limitations are not detailed in the excerpt provided [N8-R1]. Overall, the evidence suggests that the field is advancing, but it remains limited by the need for longer-term, age-comparative, region-specific, and socioeconomic research, as well as more systematic ethical, legal, and reimbursement analysis [N8-R2; N6-R1; N6-R2; N1-F1].

## 6) Bottom line: future convergence potential

Yes, there is strong potential for orthodontics and medical aesthetics to converge in the future, but the convergence is already happening unevenly rather than as a single unified market. The evidence supports several directions:

- **Clinical convergence:** multidisciplinary clinics and combined treatments are already being used, especially for complex cases where orthodontics and aesthetic outcomes are intertwined [N5-R4; N5-R5].
- **Technological convergence:** digital tools such as digital twin technology and predictive workflows are enabling more personalized and integrated planning [N5-R1; N5-R3].
- **Market convergence:** both orthodontics and aesthetic medicine are growing rapidly, with orthodontic braces and services growing at double-digit CAGR and cosmetic dentistry projected to double by 2030 [N3-R2; N3-R4; N1-R2; N1-R4].
- **Consumer convergence:** young women are increasingly using both modalities for similar drivers: self-esteem, social appearance, and career-related confidence [N2-F2; N2-R5; N4-R4; N4-R5].

At the same time, the evidence suggests that current limitations are real and important. The field lacks long-term tracking, region-specific data, and clear reimbursement and regulatory boundaries [N8-R2; N6-R1; N6-R2; N1-F1]. It also faces methodological and ethical challenges, including how outcomes are measured and how consent, transparency, and safety are ensured [N8-R3; N6-R2].

## 7) Practical conclusion

For the global 20–30-year-old female market, the best-supported conclusion is:

- **Demand is high and overlapping:** young women are increasingly seeking both orthodontic and medical aesthetic treatments, often for related reasons such as smile appearance, self-esteem, and social acceptance [N2-F2; N2-R5; N4-R4; N4-R5].
- **Proportion is hard to quantify:** the evidence does not provide a direct proportion of young women citing orthodontics versus medical aesthetics as top concerns [N2-F2; N1-R3].
- **Payment and access are shaped by price sensitivity:** many young adults are reluctant to pay premiums, but they are still spending large amounts on aesthetic procedures [N4-R1; N4-R3; N7-R2].
- **Future convergence is likely:** clinical, technological, and market trends point to stronger integration, but the field remains constrained by methodological, ethical, and regulatory gaps [N5-R4; N5-R5; N5-R1; N5-R3; N6-R1; N6-R2].

## 8) Final recommendation for your research

If you are looking for a precise answer to “what percentage of 20–30-year-old women cite orthodontics versus medical aesthetics,” the evidence does **not** support a definitive numerical answer. The strongest evidence available is qualitative and comparative: both modalities are important, they overlap in drivers, and they are both growing rapidly, especially among young women [N2-F2; N1-R3; N7-R4; N4-R4; N4-R5]. For future convergence, the evidence supports optimism, but it also warns that the field needs more rigorous longitudinal, region-specific, and reimbursement research before a clear growth forecast can be made [N8-R2; N6-R1; N6-R2; N1-F1].

Evidence on young women’s actual and perceived demand for orthodontics versus medical aesthetics

The evidence base here is uneven: it is strong on drivers of demand and social media influence, weaker on direct comparative proportions of young women citing orthodontics versus medical aesthetics, and limited on explicit 20-30-year-old female samples. The strongest direct evidence comes from aesthetic dentistry and social media studies, which show that aesthetic procedures are rising rapidly and that social media is a major driver, with teeth whitening, Hollywood smile, veneers, and Invisalign among the most commonly demanded procedures [N2-F2]. In that study, 90.7% of surveyed dentists believed demand for aesthetic procedures is increasing, and social media is a major contributor, with before-and-after pictures used for advertising [N2-F2].

For orthodontics, the evidence points to growing adult orthodontic demand and strong aesthetic motivations. A 2025 source notes that Gen Z adults prioritize aesthetics, wellness, and personal branding, making orthodontics a “natural fit for their lifestyle” [N1-R3]. A separate 2025 source states that the number of adults seeing an orthodontist is at an all-time high, with one-in-three orthodontic patients over the age of 18 [N7-R4]. That indicates broad adult orthodontic uptake, but the evidence does not specify how many young women versus young women seeking medical aesthetics are included in that trend.

On priority drivers, the evidence is consistent across sources: self-esteem, smile appearance, social pressure, and career appearance are central. The aesthetic dentistry social media study frames the demand shift as linked to social media’s power to modify self-image, with patients seeking treatments because they are trending on platforms and because celebrities and influencers appear to have “the perfect smile” [N2-F2]. Another source notes that cosmetic dental procedures provide “emotional and social advantages” by improving the appearance of teeth and boosting self-esteem [N2-R5]. The same source also links demand to self-image and the desire to “live life to it’s fullest,” showing that the perceived value is not just functional but socially expressive [N2-R2]. A separate medical aesthetics source notes that 20-somethings are paying large sums for cosmetic procedures, with motivations including self-esteem, societal standards, and preference for minimally invasive options [N4-R4]. A further source highlights work-from-home trends among 20s and 30s age groups, with more time in front of cameras and mirrors driving demand for facial fillers [N4-R5]. Taken together, these sources support a driver set centered on appearance, social acceptance, and personal branding, rather than a single dominant motive.

Evidence gaps are substantial. First, the evidence is sparse on direct comparative proportions of young women citing orthodontics versus medical aesthetics as top concerns. The available evidence is mostly aggregated at the dentist or practitioner level, not at the individual consumer level, so it cannot reliably answer “proportion of young women citing orthodontics” versus “proportion citing medical aesthetics” [N2-F2; N1-R3]. Second, the evidence is regionally limited. The aesthetic dentistry survey was conducted in a single institutional setting in Pakistan and reported 377 dentists, while the broader market sources are global in scope but do not isolate 20-30-year-old women [N2-F2; N1-R2; N1-R4]. Third, there is no explicit longitudinal data across age groups in the provided evidence, so it is hard to assess whether orthodontic and medical aesthetic demand evolves differently over time or by cohort [N1-F1; N8-R2]. Fourth, the evidence is thin on region-specific or socioeconomic variables: the female dental workforce survey covers global participation and gender dynamics, but it does not isolate young women’s treatment preferences or access barriers by region or income level [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence supports a strong demand narrative, but it is not yet sufficient to quantify a precise proportion of young women prioritizing one modality over the other.

Overall, the evidence suggests a market where young women are active and influenced by platforms, but cost, time, and social/structural barriers remain important constraints.

This suggests that the demand environment is favorable for convergence. However, the evidence on limitations is also clear. Methodological issues in clear aligner research include how outcomes are evaluated, with most studies comparing predicted and achieved tooth movement [N8-R3]. A scoping review also notes diversity in treatment types and methodological limitations, which can introduce heterogeneity and reduce generalizability [N8-R2]. The ethical and regulatory review emphasizes that aesthetic medicine has ethical dimensions and that consumer demand, societal influence, and technology are all relevant to the field [N6-R1]. It also highlights consent, confidentiality, and transparency as essential ethical care requirements [N6-R2]. Together, these limitations suggest that while the clinical and technological potential is real, the field remains constrained by methodological inconsistency, ethical complexity, and regulatory uncertainty.

## 5) Evidence gaps and limitations

The evidence points to several major gaps and limitations. First, there is a lack of longitudinal or comparative data across age groups. The provided evidence includes growth projections and market reports, but these are not longitudinal tracking studies comparing orthodontic and aesthetic demand by age over time [N1-R2; N1-R4; N3-R2; N3-R4]. The aesthetic dentistry survey is one-time and dentist-focused rather than consumer-centric, so it cannot establish age-group trends [N2-F2]. The orthodontic market reports similarly describe current or projected market size, not longitudinal cohort-level demand changes [N3-R2; N3-R4]. Second, the evidence is missing region-specific or socioeconomic data. The female dental workforce survey covers global female participation and gender dynamics, but it does not isolate young women’s treatment preferences, access, or socioeconomic barriers [N1-F1]. The medical aesthetics and orthodontic sources are global in scope but do not break out data by region, income level, or cultural context [N4-R1; N4-R3; N4-R4; N7-R4]. Third, ethical, legal, and reimbursement boundaries are not fully documented in the provided evidence. The ethical review discusses consumer demand, societal influences, and technology, but it does not provide a comprehensive reimbursement analysis [N6-R1]. The legal considerations source mentions consent, confidentiality, and transparency as ethical requirements, but it does not address legal liability, insurance coverage, or reimbursement policy differences across countries [N6-R2]. The Nuffield Council on Bioethics and other ethical sources highlight broader concerns about cosmetic procedures, but again, the evidence provided does not synthesize reimbursement or legal frameworks across jurisdictions [N6-R4; N6-R5].

The methodological limitations are also important. The scoping review notes that including a variety of TMD types and combinations can introduce heterogeneity and reduce comparability [N8-R2]. The clear aligner research source states that core methodological concerns are how outcomes are evaluated, particularly comparisons of predicted versus achieved tooth movement [N8-R3]. The aesthetic and orthodontic treatment desires study notes psychosocial impacts and relationships with treatment desire, but its limitations are not detailed in the excerpt provided [N8-R1]. Overall, the evidence suggests that the field is advancing, but it remains limited by the need for longer-term, age-comparative, region-specific, and socioeconomic research, as well as more systematic ethical, legal, and reimbursement analysis [N8-R2; N6-R1; N6-R2; N1-F1].

## 6) Bottom line: future convergence potential

Yes, there is strong potential for orthodontics and medical aesthetics to converge in the future, but the convergence is already happening unevenly rather than as a single unified market. The evidence supports several directions:

- **Clinical convergence:** multidisciplinary clinics and combined treatments are already being used, especially for complex cases where orthodontics and aesthetic outcomes are intertwined [N5-R4; N5-R5].
- **Technological convergence:** digital tools such as digital twin technology and predictive workflows are enabling more personalized and integrated planning [N5-R1; N5-R3].
- **Market convergence:** both orthodontics and aesthetic medicine are growing rapidly, with orthodontic braces and services growing at double-digit CAGR and cosmetic dentistry projected to double by 2030 [N3-R2; N3-R4; N1-R2; N1-R4].
- **Consumer convergence:** young women are increasingly using both modalities for similar drivers: self-esteem, social appearance, and career-related confidence [N2-F2; N2-R5; N4-R4; N4-R5].

At the same time, the evidence suggests that current limitations are real and important. The field lacks long-term tracking, region-specific data, and clear reimbursement and regulatory boundaries [N8-R2; N6-R1; N6-R2; N1-F1]. It also faces methodological and ethical challenges, including how outcomes are measured and how consent, transparency, and safety are ensured [N8-R3; N6-R2].

## 7) Practical conclusion

For the global 20–30-year-old female market, the best-supported conclusion is:

- **Demand is high and overlapping:** young women are increasingly seeking both orthodontic and medical aesthetic treatments, often for related reasons such as smile appearance, self-esteem, and social acceptance [N2-F2; N2-R5; N4-R4; N4-R5].
- **Proportion is hard to quantify:** the evidence does not provide a direct proportion of young women citing orthodontics versus medical aesthetics as top concerns [N2-F2; N1-R3].
- **Payment and access are shaped by price sensitivity:** many young adults are reluctant to pay premiums, but they are still spending large amounts on aesthetic procedures [N4-R1; N4-R3; N7-R2].
- **Future convergence is likely:** clinical, technological, and market trends point to stronger integration, but the field remains constrained by methodological, ethical, and regulatory gaps [N5-R4; N5-R5; N5-R1; N5-R3; N6-R1; N6-R2].

## 8) Final recommendation for your research

If you are looking for a precise answer to “what percentage of 20–30-year-old women cite orthodontics versus medical aesthetics,” the evidence does **not** support a definitive numerical answer. The strongest evidence available is qualitative and comparative: both modalities are important, they overlap in drivers, and they are both growing rapidly, especially among young women [N2-F2; N1-R3; N7-R4; N4-R4; N4-R5]. For future convergence, the evidence supports optimism, but it also warns that the field needs more rigorous longitudinal, region-specific, and reimbursement research before a clear growth forecast can be made [N8-R2; N6-R1; N6-R2; N1-F1].
